source_user: Advanced cluster case cluster scheduling and recovery-26: Design a resilient cluster scheduler for distributed LLM training and inference. Variant 26 must state assumptions, define a falsifiable hypothesis, name metrics, and include one failure or rollback condition.
source_assistant: An expert answer should distinguish model-domain mechanisms from runtime measurements. Required technical anchors: cover gang scheduling, GPU/NIC/topology-aware placement, fragmentation, preemption, checkpoint cadence, node drain, elastic restart, replica routing, SLOs, and resource accounting. It must report topology, workload, units, baselines, confounders, and evidence needed before claiming improvement.
corrected_answer:
For variant 26, treat resilience as a falsifiable scheduler-and-recovery property, not an assumed platform capability. Assumptions: jobs declare GPU type/count, CPU, memory, storage, NIC/RDMA, NUMA/topology, DP/TP shape, priority, checkpoint format and interval, and inference SLOs; inventory, placement, preemption, fencing, routing, and failure events are observable; actual capacities and recovery semantics must be measured.

Hypothesis: topology-aware gang admission with fragmentation-aware packing, checkpoint-aware preemption, and bounded node-drain recovery will reduce wasted GPU-hours and p95 recovery time without worsening inference availability or latency, compared with the current first-fit policy. Hold workload mix, model, cluster inventory, checkpoint policy, and replica-routing policy fixed in matched baseline/canary windows.

Design: admit distributed jobs atomically when their GPU/NIC/NUMA constraints fit; otherwise expose queue reason and fragmentation rather than partially starting a gang. Reserve topology-compatible capacity, account CPU, memory, storage, GPU-hours, and network capacity, and preempt only policy-eligible work after a consistent checkpoint. On drain or failure, fence the node, verify checkpoint integrity, restart elastically only if the parallelism contract permits it, and route inference replicas away from unhealthy or overloaded capacity. Never claim fencing or elastic semantics without platform evidence.

Measure queue/admission time (s), placement failures, fragmentation (GPU-hours unavailable to requested shapes), GPU/NIC utilization (%), checkpoint interval and size (s/GB), preemption loss (GPU-hours), node-drain and recovery time (s), restart count, duplicate/lost work, request p50/p95/p99 latency (ms), error rate (%), availability (%), SLO violations, and resource-accounting error (%). Synchronize clocks, define sampling windows, report distributions and confidence intervals, and compare against a matched baseline; stratify by job shape, topology, priority, and failure type. Confounders include load mix, thermal or fabric faults, checkpoint storage, scheduler retries, replica warmup, autoscaling, and unrelated software changes.

For this performance analysis prompt, collect scheduler events, topology/inventory snapshots, checkpoint manifests, node-fencing evidence, routing decisions, and redacted traces. Canary with least privilege and an explicit stop gate: rollback if fencing is unverified, checkpoint integrity fails, recovery exceeds the tested bound, accounting diverges, or any agreed inference SLO regresses. Evidence is required before generalizing beyond the measured cluster, workload, and failure injection; do not expose credentials or claim expert validation.
risks: platform-specific scheduler, fencing, checkpoint, and elastic-restart semantics may differ
synthetic prompt lacks measured cluster topology and baseline data
controlled failure injection can affect availability if isolation is inadequate
evidence_required: matched baseline/canary telemetry with units and synchronized timestamps
